blocks.tex:
In $\R^m$ the Heine–Borel theorem says a set is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. In the function space $C^0[a,b]$ this fails: the sequence $x^n$ lies in the closed unit ball of $C^0[0,1]$ and has no uniformly convergent subsequence. The missing ingredient is a condition that keeps all the functions in the set from oscillating too wildly, \emph{equicontinuity}. With it, bounded sequences do have uniformly convergent subsequences (the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem), and compact subsets of $C^0$ are exactly the closed, bounded, equicontinuous ones.

In this section compactness of a metric space is used in its sequential form: every sequence has a subsequence converging to a point of the space. (By Chapter 2 this is equivalent to covering compactness, which the next section uses.)

blocks.title: Equicontinuity
blocks.tex:
Let $M$ be a metric space with metric $d$ and let $\mathcal{E}$ be a set of functions $M \to \R$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathcal{E}$ is \emph{equicontinuous} if for every $\eps > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and all $s, t \in M$,
\[ d(s,t) < \delta \implies \abs{f(s) - f(t)} < \eps . \]
\item $\mathcal{E}$ is \emph{pointwise equicontinuous} if for every $p \in M$ and every $\eps > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and all $x \in M$, $d(x,p) < \delta$ implies $\abs{f(x) - f(p)} < \eps$.
\end{itemize}
A sequence $(f_n)$ is called (pointwise) equicontinuous if the set $\set{f_n : n \in \N}$ is. In equicontinuity one $\delta$ serves all functions and all points; in pointwise equicontinuity $\delta$ may depend on $p$ but still not on $f$. Each member of an equicontinuous set is uniformly continuous.

A subset $\mathcal{E}$ of $C_b(M)$ is \emph{bounded} if there is a constant $B$ with $\norm{f} \le B$ for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$; this is boundedness in the sup metric, and is also called \emph{uniform boundedness}.

blocks.title: The powers $x^n$ are not equicontinuous
blocks.tex: The sequence $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0,1]$ is bounded in $C^0[0,1]$ but is not equicontinuous.
blocks.proof:
$\norm{f_n} = 1$ for all $n$, so the sequence is bounded.

Take $\eps = \tfrac12$ and let $\delta > 0$ be arbitrary. Put $t = \max(0, 1 - \delta/2)$, so $t \in [0,1)$ and $\abs{1 - t} \le \delta/2 < \delta$. Since $0 \le t < 1$, $t^n \to 0$, so there is an $n$ with $t^n < \tfrac12$. For this $n$,
\[ \abs{f_n(1) - f_n(t)} = 1 - t^n > \tfrac12 = \eps \]
although $\abs{1 - t} < \delta$. So no $\delta$ works for $\eps = \tfrac12$, and the sequence is not equicontinuous.
hints: Negate the definition: find one $\eps$ such that for every $\delta$ some $f_n$ changes by at least $\eps$ between two points closer than $\delta$.
Look near $x = 1$: fix $t < 1$ close to $1$ and let $n$ grow.

blocks.title: A common Lipschitz constant gives equicontinuity
blocks.tex:
Let $M$ be a metric space, $L \ge 0$, and let $\mathcal{E}$ be a set of functions $M \to \R$ such that $\abs{f(s) - f(t)} \le L\, d(s,t)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and $s,t \in M$. Then $\mathcal{E}$ is equicontinuous.

In particular, if $\mathcal{E}$ is a set of differentiable functions $[a,b] \to \R$ with $\abs{f'(x)} \le L$ for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and all $x \in [a,b]$, then $\mathcal{E}$ is equicontinuous.
blocks.proof:
Let $\eps > 0$ and put $\delta = \eps/(L+1)$. If $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and $d(s,t) < \delta$ then $\abs{f(s) - f(t)} \le L\,d(s,t) \le L\delta < \eps$. So $\mathcal{E}$ is equicontinuous.

For the second statement let $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and $s < t$ in $[a,b]$. By the mean value theorem there is a $\theta \in (s,t)$ with $f(t) - f(s) = f'(\theta)(t - s)$, so $\abs{f(t) - f(s)} \le L\abs{t - s}$; this also holds trivially when $s = t$ and by symmetry when $s > t$. So the first statement applies.
hints: Choose $\delta$ in terms of $\eps$ and $L$ only. For the second part, the mean value theorem converts a bound on $f'$ into a Lipschitz bound.

blocks.title: A uniformly convergent sequence is equicontinuous
blocks.tex: Let $M$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(f_n)$ be a sequence in $C^0(M)$ that converges uniformly on $M$. Then $(f_n)$ is equicontinuous. Also, every finite subset of $C^0(M)$ is equicontinuous.
blocks.proof:
Recall that a continuous real function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.

\emph{Finite sets.} Let $g_1,\dots,g_k \in C^0(M)$ and $\eps > 0$. Each $g_i$ is uniformly continuous, so there is $\delta_i > 0$ with $\abs{g_i(s) - g_i(t)} < \eps$ whenever $d(s,t) < \delta_i$. Then $\delta = \min(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k) > 0$ works for all $g_i$.

\emph{Uniformly convergent sequences.} Let $f_n \rightrightarrows f$. Then $f$ is continuous, being a uniform limit of continuous functions, hence uniformly continuous on $M$. Let $\eps > 0$. Choose $N$ with $\abs{f_n(x) - f(x)} < \eps/3$ for all $n \ge N$ and all $x \in M$, and $\delta_0 > 0$ with $\abs{f(s) - f(t)} < \eps/3$ whenever $d(s,t) < \delta_0$. For $n \ge N$ and $d(s,t) < \delta_0$,
\[ \abs{f_n(s) - f_n(t)} \le \abs{f_n(s) - f(s)} + \abs{f(s) - f(t)} + \abs{f(t) - f_n(t)} < \eps . \]
If $N = 1$ there are no further indices and $\delta = \delta_0$ works for every $n$. Otherwise, by the finite case applied to $f_1, \dots, f_{N-1}$, there is $\delta_1 > 0$ such that $\abs{f_n(s) - f_n(t)} < \eps$ whenever $d(s,t) < \delta_1$ and $n < N$; then $\delta = \min(\delta_0,\delta_1)$ works for every $n$.
hints: Handle the tail of the sequence and the finitely many initial terms separately.
For $n \ge N$ compare $f_n$ with the limit $f$, which is uniformly continuous because $M$ is compact; three terms of size $\eps/3$.

blocks.title: On a compact space, pointwise equicontinuity is equicontinuity
blocks.tex: Let $M$ be a compact metric space and $\mathcal{E}$ a pointwise equicontinuous set of functions $M \to \R$. Then $\mathcal{E}$ is equicontinuous.
blocks.proof:
Suppose not. Then there is an $\eps > 0$ such that for every $k \in \N$ the choice $\delta = 1/k$ fails: there are $f_k \in \mathcal{E}$ and $s_k, t_k \in M$ with $d(s_k,t_k) < 1/k$ and $\abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(t_k)} \ge \eps$.

By compactness a subsequence $(s_{k_j})$ converges to some $p \in M$. Since $d(t_{k_j}, p) \le d(t_{k_j}, s_{k_j}) + d(s_{k_j}, p) < 1/k_j + d(s_{k_j},p) \to 0$, also $t_{k_j} \to p$.

By pointwise equicontinuity at $p$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $\abs{f(x) - f(p)} < \eps/2$ for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$ and all $x$ with $d(x,p) < \delta$. Choose $j$ so large that $d(s_{k_j},p) < \delta$ and $d(t_{k_j},p) < \delta$. Then with $k = k_j$,
\[ \abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(t_k)} \le \abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(p)} + \abs{f_k(p) - f_k(t_k)} < \frac{\eps}{2} + \frac{\eps}{2} = \eps , \]
contradicting $\abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(t_k)} \ge \eps$.
hints: Argue by contradiction, exactly as in the proof that a continuous function on a compact space is uniformly continuous.
Get bad triples $(f_k, s_k, t_k)$ with $d(s_k,t_k) < 1/k$; pass to a subsequence with $s_k \to p$ and use pointwise equicontinuity at the single point $p$.

blocks.title: Finite nets and a countable dense subset
blocks.proof:
If $M$ is empty take $F = \emptyset$ and $D = \emptyset$; so let $M$ be nonempty.

(1) Suppose that for some $r > 0$ no such finite set exists. Choose $x_1 \in M$. Having chosen $x_1,\dots,x_n$, the finite set $\set{x_1,\dots,x_n}$ does not have the required property, so there is a point $x_{n+1} \in M$ with $d(x_{n+1}, x_i) \ge r$ for all $i \le n$. This produces a sequence with $d(x_m, x_n) \ge r$ whenever $m \ne n$. No subsequence of it is Cauchy, hence no subsequence converges, contradicting the compactness of $M$.

(2) For each $n \in \N$ let $F_n$ be a finite set as in (1) with $r = 1/n$, and let $D = \bigcup_{n} F_n$, a countable union of finite sets and therefore countable. Given $x \in M$ and $\eps > 0$, choose $n$ with $1/n < \eps$; some point of $F_n \subseteq D$ lies within $1/n < \eps$ of $x$. So $D$ is dense in $M$.
hints: For (1), if no finite set works, build a sequence whose points are pairwise at least $r$ apart.
For (2), take the union of finite $1/n$-nets over all $n$.

blocks.title: Diagonal subsequence
blocks.tex: Let $D$ be a countable set and let $f_n : D \to \R$ $(n \in \N)$ be functions such that for each $x \in D$ the sequence of numbers $(f_n(x))_{n}$ is bounded. Then there is a subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ such that $(f_{n_k}(x))_k$ converges for every $x \in D$.
blocks.proof:
If $D$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise list the points of $D$ as $d_1, d_2, d_3, \dots$ (repeating points if $D$ is finite).

We construct infinite sets of indices $\N = A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ such that, for each $j \ge 1$, the numbers $f_n(d_j)$ converge as $n \to \infty$ through $A_j$. Suppose $A_{j-1}$ has been constructed. The sequence $(f_n(d_j))_{n \in A_{j-1}}$ (indices in increasing order) is bounded, so by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem it has a convergent subsequence; let $A_j \subseteq A_{j-1}$ be the infinite set of indices of that subsequence.

Now choose $n_1 \in A_1$ and, inductively, $n_k \in A_k$ with $n_k > n_{k-1}$; this is possible because $A_k$ is infinite. Then $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$, so $(f_{n_k})$ is a subsequence of $(f_n)$.

Fix $j$. For $k \ge j$ we have $n_k \in A_k \subseteq A_j$, and the $n_k$ are strictly increasing, so $(f_{n_k}(d_j))_{k \ge j}$ is a subsequence of the convergent sequence $(f_n(d_j))_{n \in A_j}$. Hence $(f_{n_k}(d_j))_k$ converges. Since every point of $D$ is some $d_j$, the subsequence converges at every point of $D$.
hints: Handle the points of $D$ one at a time: Bolzano–Weierstrass gives a subsequence converging at $d_1$, then a further subsequence converging at $d_2$, and so on.
No single one of these nested subsequences works for all points. Take the $k$-th term of the $k$-th subsequence (the diagonal): from the $j$-th term on it is a subsequence of the $j$-th one.

blocks.title: Arzelà–Ascoli propagation theorem
blocks.tex: Let $M$ be a compact metric space, $D$ a dense subset of $M$, and $(f_n)$ an equicontinuous sequence of functions $M \to \R$ such that $(f_n(x))$ converges for every $x \in D$. Then $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $M$.
blocks.proof:
By the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence it suffices to show that $(f_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy. Let $\eps > 0$.

By equicontinuity there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $\abs{f_n(s) - f_n(t)} < \eps/3$ for all $n$ whenever $d(s,t) < \delta$.

By the lemma on finite nets there are points $x_1,\dots,x_J \in M$ such that every point of $M$ is within $\delta/2$ of some $x_j$. Since $D$ is dense, for each $j$ there is a $d_j \in D$ with $d(d_j, x_j) < \delta/2$. Then every $x \in M$ satisfies $d(x, d_j) \le d(x,x_j) + d(x_j,d_j) < \delta$ for some $j \in \set{1,\dots,J}$.

For each $j$ the sequence $(f_n(d_j))_n$ converges, hence is Cauchy, so there is an $N_j$ with $\abs{f_m(d_j) - f_n(d_j)} < \eps/3$ for $m,n \ge N_j$. Let $N = \max(N_1,\dots,N_J)$.

Now let $m, n \ge N$ and $x \in M$, and pick $j$ with $d(x,d_j) < \delta$. Then
\[ \abs{f_m(x) - f_n(x)} \le \abs{f_m(x) - f_m(d_j)} + \abs{f_m(d_j) - f_n(d_j)} + \abs{f_n(d_j) - f_n(x)} < \frac{\eps}{3} + \frac{\eps}{3} + \frac{\eps}{3} = \eps . \]
So $(f_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy, and therefore converges uniformly on $M$. (If $M$ is empty the statement is vacuous.)
hints: You do not know the limit off $D$, so prove that $(f_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy.
Equicontinuity gives a $\delta$ for $\eps/3$. Use compactness and density to find \emph{finitely many} points of $D$ such that every point of $M$ is within $\delta$ of one of them.
At finitely many points the sequences are simultaneously Cauchy from some $N$ on. Then estimate $\abs{f_m(x) - f_n(x)}$ by passing through a nearby $d_j$.

blocks.title: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem
blocks.tex: Let $M$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every bounded, equicontinuous sequence $(f_n)$ in $C^0(M)$ has a subsequence that converges uniformly on $M$; its limit belongs to $C^0(M)$. In particular this holds for $M = [a,b]$.
blocks.proof:
By the lemma on finite nets $M$ has a countable dense subset $D$. Let $B$ be a bound: $\norm{f_n} \le B$ for all $n$. Then for each $x \in D$ the sequence $(f_n(x))$ is bounded by $B$, so by the diagonal subsequence lemma (applied to the restrictions of the $f_n$ to $D$) there is a subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ such that $(f_{n_k}(x))_k$ converges for every $x \in D$.

The subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ is still equicontinuous, since the same $\delta$ works for a subset of the functions. By the propagation theorem it converges uniformly on $M$. Its limit is continuous because a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
hints: Three ingredients are already available: a countable dense set, the diagonal subsequence lemma, and the propagation theorem.
Boundedness gives pointwise bounded sequences on the dense set $D$; extract a subsequence converging at every point of $D$; then propagate.

blocks.title: Bounded derivatives
blocks.tex: Let $f_n : [a,b] \to \R$ be differentiable functions and suppose there are constants $L$ and $C$ and a point $x_0 \in [a,b]$ such that $\abs{f_n'(x)} \le L$ for all $n$ and all $x \in [a,b]$, and $\abs{f_n(x_0)} \le C$ for all $n$. Then $(f_n)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
blocks.proof:
Each $f_n$ is differentiable, hence continuous, so $f_n \in C^0[a,b]$. A set of differentiable functions whose derivatives are bounded by a common constant $L$ is equicontinuous, and moreover (by the mean value theorem, as in that proposition) $\abs{f_n(x) - f_n(x_0)} \le L\abs{x - x_0}$. Hence for all $n$ and $x$,
\[ \abs{f_n(x)} \le \abs{f_n(x_0)} + L\abs{x - x_0} \le C + L(b-a) , \]
so the sequence is bounded in $C^0[a,b]$. The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a uniformly convergent subsequence.
hints: Check the two hypotheses of Arzelà–Ascoli. The bound on the derivatives gives equicontinuity; what gives boundedness?

blocks.title: Heine–Borel theorem in a function space
blocks.tex: Let $M$ be a nonempty compact metric space. A subset $\mathcal{E} \subseteq C^0(M)$ is compact (in the sup metric) if and only if it is closed, bounded and equicontinuous.
blocks.proof:
\emph{Closed, bounded, equicontinuous implies compact.} Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{E}$. It is bounded and equicontinuous, so by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem a subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ converges uniformly to some $f \in C^0(M)$, i.e. $\norm{f_{n_k} - f} \to 0$. Since $\mathcal{E}$ is closed in $C^0(M)$, $f \in \mathcal{E}$. So every sequence in $\mathcal{E}$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $\mathcal{E}$.

\emph{Compact implies closed, bounded, equicontinuous.} A compact subset of any metric space is closed and bounded; bounded here means contained in some ball about a function $g \in C^0(M)$ of some radius $\rho$ in the sup metric, and then $\norm{f} \le \norm{g} + \rho$ for all $f \in \mathcal{E}$. (If $\mathcal{E}$ is empty all three properties hold trivially.)

Suppose $\mathcal{E}$ is not equicontinuous. Then there is an $\eps > 0$ such that for each $k \in \N$ there are $f_k \in \mathcal{E}$ and $s_k, t_k \in M$ with
\[ d(s_k, t_k) < 1/k \quad \text{and} \quad \abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(t_k)} \ge \eps . \]
By compactness of $\mathcal{E}$ a subsequence $(f_{k_j})_j$ converges in the sup metric, that is uniformly, to some $f \in \mathcal{E}$. A uniformly convergent sequence in $C^0(M)$ is equicontinuous, so there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $\abs{f_{k_j}(s) - f_{k_j}(t)} < \eps$ for all $j$ whenever $d(s,t) < \delta$. Choose $j$ with $1/k_j < \delta$. Then $d(s_{k_j}, t_{k_j}) < \delta$, so $\abs{f_{k_j}(s_{k_j}) - f_{k_j}(t_{k_j})} < \eps$, contradicting the choice of $f_{k_j}, s_{k_j}, t_{k_j}$. Hence $\mathcal{E}$ is equicontinuous.
hints: One direction is Arzelà–Ascoli plus closedness. For the other, closed and bounded come for free from compactness; equicontinuity is the real content.
If $\mathcal{E}$ is not equicontinuous, get $f_k \in \mathcal{E}$ and points $s_k, t_k$ with $d(s_k,t_k) < 1/k$ but $\abs{f_k(s_k) - f_k(t_k)} \ge \eps$.
Compactness gives a uniformly convergent subsequence of $(f_k)$, and a uniformly convergent sequence of continuous functions on a compact space is equicontinuous.

blocks.title: The closed unit ball of $C^0[0,1]$ is not compact
blocks.tex: Let $\mathcal{B} = \set{ f \in C^0[0,1] : \norm{f} \le 1 }$. Then $\mathcal{B}$ is closed and bounded in $C^0[0,1]$, but it is not compact.
blocks.proof:
$\mathcal{B}$ is bounded by definition. It is closed: if $f_n \in \mathcal{B}$ and $
orm{f_n - f} 	o 0$ with $f \in C^0[0,1]$, then $
orm{f} \le 
orm{f - f_n} + 
orm{f_n} \le 
orm{f - f_n} + 1$ for every $n$, and letting $n 	o \infty$ gives $
orm{f} \le 1$.

The functions $f_n(x) = x^n$ belong to $\mathcal{B}$. Suppose some subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ converged in the sup metric to a function $g \in C^0[0,1]$. Then $f_{n_k} ightrightarrows g$, hence $f_{n_k} 	o g$ pointwise. But $x^{n_k} 	o 0$ for $0 \le x < 1$ and $1^{n_k} 	o 1$, so $g(x) = 0$ for $x < 1$ and $g(1) = 1$, which is not continuous at $1$ — a contradiction with $g \in C^0[0,1]$. So $(f_n)$ has no subsequence converging in $C^0[0,1]$, and $\mathcal{B}$ is not compact.

(Alternatively: $\mathcal{B}$ contains the sequence $(x^n)$, which is not equicontinuous, so $\mathcal{B}$ is not equicontinuous and the Heine–Borel theorem in a function space applies.)
hints: Exhibit a sequence in the ball with no uniformly convergent subsequence.
Try $x^n$: any uniform limit of a subsequence would have to equal the pointwise limit, which is discontinuous.

cards.front: Define: the set $\mathcal{E}$ of functions $M \to \R$ is equicontinuous.
cards.back: For every $\eps>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $d(s,t)<\delta$ implies $\abs{f(s)-f(t)}<\eps$ for all $s,t \in M$ and all $f \in \mathcal{E}$: one $\delta$ for all points and all functions.

cards.front: Give a simple sufficient condition for equicontinuity, and a bounded sequence in $C^0[0,1]$ that is not equicontinuous.
cards.back: A common Lipschitz constant, e.g. differentiable functions with $\abs{f'} \le L$. Not equicontinuous: $x^n$ (near $x=1$), or $\sin(nx)$.
If $M$ is compact, every bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C^0(M)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence.

cards.front: Outline the proof of the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem in three steps.
cards.back: (1) $M$ has a countable dense subset $D$. (2) Diagonal argument with Bolzano–Weierstrass: a subsequence converges at every point of $D$. (3) Propagation: equicontinuity plus a finite $\delta$-net of points of $D$ makes the subsequence uniformly Cauchy on $M$.
On a compact metric space, an equicontinuous sequence that converges pointwise on a dense subset converges uniformly on the whole space.

cards.front: Which subsets of $C^0(M)$, $M$ compact, are compact?
cards.back: Exactly the closed, bounded, equicontinuous ones. Closed and bounded is not enough: the closed unit ball of $C^0[0,1]$ contains $x^n$, which has no uniformly convergent subsequence.

cards.front: What does the diagonal subsequence lemma say, and what is the trick?
cards.back: A sequence of functions that is bounded at each point of a countable set $D$ has a subsequence converging at every point of $D$. Take nested subsequences converging at $d_1$, then $d_2$, …, and pick the $k$-th term of the $k$-th one.
